captions.instagram:
How do fish swim?

A fish never paddles: it bends. Watch a wave run down a rohu's body, see the swirls its tail leaves behind, and find out how a bag of gas lets it hang still in the water.

→ Most of a fish is muscle, cut into W-shaped blocks along a flexible backbone.
→ A fish swims by bending: a wave runs down its body and grows towards the tail.
→ Every flick sheds a swirl, and a jet of water between them pushes the fish forward.
→ Eels bend all over, tunas flick just the tail, and good swimmers keep Strouhal near 0.3.
→ A swim bladder is a bag of gas: dive deeper and the water squeezes it smaller.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/fishswimclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How do fish swim? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A fish never paddles: it bends. Watch a wave run down a rohu's body, see the swirls its tail leaves behind, and find out how a bag of gas lets it hang still in the water.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/fishswimclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/fishswimclear

In this video:
• Most of a fish is muscle. A fish's body is mostly swimming muscle, cut into W-shaped blocks called myomeres along a bendy backbone.
• A wave runs down the body. Muscles shorten one block after another, first on one side, then the other.
• A bag of gas to hang still. Fish flesh is a little denser than water.
• India's fish. Catla, rohu and mrigal share Indian ponds by feeding at the top, middle and bottom.
• Fish and people. A fish stock gives the biggest steady catch when it is kept at about half its natural size.
• How we found out. Breder sorted swimming styles in 1926, Gray filmed eels in 1933 and posed his dolphin paradox in 1936, Lighthill wrote the maths in 1960, and robot fish have tested the ideas since 1994.
